questions.stem: Which of the following best describes an example of implicit bias in an informational text?

options.label: A
options.text: Using words like "disastrous" and "horrifying" to describe an event.
options.feedbackWrong: This is explicit bias because the language is openly opinionated and inflammatory.

options.label: B
options.text: Presenting only data that supports one side of an argument while omitting contrary evidence.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Implicit bias often works through omission or one-sided framing rather than obvious emotional words.

options.label: C
options.text: Stating "The mayor made a terrible decision" without providing reasons.
options.feedbackWrong: This is an explicit opinion, not implicit bias. The author directly states the judgment.

options.label: D
options.text: Including a headline that says "Shocking Revelation Uncovered!"
options.feedbackWrong: Sensational headlines may grab attention but don't necessarily indicate implicit bias; they are often explicit.

questions.learningGoal: Distinguish between explicit and implicit bias.
questions.successCriteria: Correctly identifies implicit bias as omission or one-sided framing.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
questions.alignmentNote: Directly addresses reading strategies to detect implicit bias.
questions.stemIntent: Checks if student understands bias is not only explicit but also implicit via omission.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think bias only appears as explicitly opinionated language.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between denotation and connotation, and provide an example of a word whose connotation could change the reader's perception of a news event compared to a neutral synonym.
questions.rubric: Response must define denotation (literal meaning) and connotation (emotional association), give an example (e.g., "thrifty" vs "cheap"), and explain how the connotation influences perception.
questions.sampleStrongAnswer: Denotation is the dictionary definition; connotation is the feeling a word evokes. For example, describing a politician as "shrewd" suggests cleverness positively, while "cunning" implies deceit. In a news article, choosing "shrewd" frames the politician more favorably.
questions.learningGoal: Analyze how authors use connotation to shape reader perception.
questions.successCriteria: Student correctly defines denotation and connotation and provides a relevant example with explanation.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
questions.alignmentNote: Assesses understanding of language choices in texts.
questions.stemIntent: Checks ability to distinguish between literal and associative word meanings.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may conflate denotation and connotation, treating all word meanings as purely literal.

questions.stem:
Read the following short passage.

"First, mix the dry ingredients. Next, add the wet ingredients and stir until combined. Then, bake at 350°F for 20 minutes. Finally, let cool before serving."

This passage primarily uses which text structure?

options.label: A
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The passage uses time-order words ("First," "Next," "Then," "Finally") to sequence steps.

options.label: B
options.feedbackWrong: Cause and effect would explain why something happens and its result. This passage simply lists steps in order.

options.label: C
options.feedbackWrong: Problem-solution would present a problem and propose a solution. There is no problem stated here.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: Compare and contrast would highlight similarities and differences between two or more things.

questions.learningGoal: Identify common informational text structures such as chronological order, cause/effect, and problem/solution.
questions.successCriteria: Correctly identifies chronological order from signal words like "first", "next", "then".
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.
questions.stemIntent: Tests ability to distinguish between text structures like chronological vs cause-effect.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may confuse chronological order with process/sequence or cause-effect when causal language is absent.

questions.stem:
Given this short passage:

"The mayor's decision to cut school funding was a heartless move that will devastate the community's future. In reality, proper funding could have been maintained if the council had prioritized education over vanity projects."

Is this objective reporting or perspective-driven prose? Justify your answer with two specific reasons from the text.
questions.rubric: Must identify as perspective-driven; reasons include use of loaded language ("heartless", "devastate"), value judgment without evidence, and one-sided attribution of motive.
questions.sampleStrongAnswer: This is perspective-driven prose. The author uses emotionally charged words like "heartless" and "devastate" that indicate opinion. Also, the claim about "vanity projects" is presented as fact without citation, showing selective evidence to fault the council.
questions.learningGoal: Distinguish between objective reporting and perspective-driven prose using textual evidence.
questions.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies text type and provides two valid reasons from the text.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.
questions.alignmentNote: Assesses ability to recognize textual features of opinion vs fact.
questions.stemIntent: Checks if student can differentiate objective from subjective writing by analyzing language.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may assume all informational texts are objective and miss value-laden language.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an appropriate use of an AI tool for a critical reading assignment?

options.label: A
options.text: Asking the AI to write a full analysis essay and submitting it as your own work.
options.feedbackWrong: Submitting AI-generated work as your own is plagiarism and academically dishonest.

options.label: B
options.text: Using the AI to generate fake citations to support your argument.
options.feedbackWrong: Fabricating citations is a serious form of academic misconduct, even if generated by AI.

options.label: C
options.text: Asking the AI to explain the difference between explicit and implicit bias to help you understand the concept.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Using AI as a learning aid to clarify concepts is ethical, as long as the final submitted work is your own.

options.label: D
options.text: Copying an AI-generated summary of a text and presenting it as your own analysis.
options.feedbackWrong: Presenting AI-generated content as original work is a violation of academic integrity.

questions.learningGoal: Explain appropriate and ethical uses of AI in critical reading tasks.
questions.successCriteria: Selects the option that uses AI as a learning partner without substituting for original work.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of their own roles and responsibilities in the learning process.
questions.alignmentNote: AI use ties to student responsibility for own learning and academic honesty.
questions.stemIntent: Checks understanding that AI should support learning, not replace it.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think using AI to generate complete work is acceptable.

reteachModules.trigger: A student flags bias only when they see words like 'terrible' or 'disastrous', but does not notice when a text excludes opposing evidence or frames an issue from only one side.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Bias only exists when the author uses openly opinionated, inflammatory language; neutral-sounding texts are automatically unbiased.

miniLesson.explain: Bias is not limited to emotional language. Explicit bias is obvious: it uses openly opinionated or inflammatory words. Implicit bias is subtle: it may omit facts or present a one-sided framing that steers the reader. To catch implicit bias, you must verify against other sources and ask what information might be missing.
miniLesson.example: An article says: 'The new plaza will bring jobs and shoppers.' It quotes only the developer, never local residents. No harsh words appear, but leaving out the other side makes it implicitly biased. A cross-source check would reveal resident complaints about traffic and noise.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Explicit bias shouts; implicit bias hides. If no angry words appear, ask what was left out.

guidedPractice.prompt: Label each sentence as showing explicit or implicit bias. A: 'This reckless plan will destroy our town.' B: 'The plan has many benefits; some residents have raised concerns.'
guidedPractice.answer: A is explicit bias because 'reckless' and 'destroy' are openly opinionated and inflammatory. B is implicit bias because it acknowledges concerns vaguely but frames the plan positively and omits specific opposition.

guidedPractice.prompt: A news report on a new factory quotes company officials praising job creation but does not mention environmental groups' objections, even though they held a protest. Is this explicit or implicit bias? Explain what was omitted.
guidedPractice.answer: Implicit bias. The report omits the environmental groups' protests and quotes only supportive voices, creating one-sided framing. No inflammatory language is used, but the missing perspective shapes readers.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write one sentence with explicit bias and one sentence with implicit bias about the same event (a mayor's decision to build a library), based on the fact bank's distinction, then explain the difference.
guidedPractice.answer: Explicit: 'The mayor's absurd library plan is a waste of taxpayer money.' Implicit: 'The new library project is expected to bring many benefits to the community.' (quotes only supporters and omits critics). Explicit bias uses openly opinionated, inflammatory language; implicit bias uses omission and one-sided framing.

reteachModules.trigger: When a student encounters a word in an informational text and treats it as purely neutral or dictionary-defined, missing the emotional weight the author has chosen.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may conflate denotation and connotation, treating all word meanings as purely literal and ignoring emotional associations.

miniLesson.explain: Denotation is a word's literal dictionary meaning, while connotation is its emotional or cultural association. Authors choose words to shape reader perception, so a single word can carry an implicit judgment that goes beyond its dictionary definition.
miniLesson.example: Consider 'thrifty' versus 'cheap'. Both denote carefulness with money, but 'thrifty' implies a positive trait, while 'cheap' suggests stinginess. An author describing a character as 'thrifty' creates a favorable impression, whereas 'cheap' creates a negative one.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Denotation is the dictionary meaning; connotation is the emotional echo.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the difference between denotation and connotation?
guidedPractice.answer: Denotation is the literal dictionary meaning; connotation is the emotional or cultural association.

guidedPractice.prompt: Why might an author choose 'slim' instead of 'skinny' to describe a person? How does connotation affect the reader's perception?
guidedPractice.answer: 'Slim' has a positive connotation (fit, attractive) while 'skinny' has a negative or neutral one (too thin). The author's choice shapes how readers view the person, showing how connotation can influence perception.

guidedPractice.prompt: Analyze the sentence: 'The mayor's decision was bold, while opponents called it reckless.' Explain how connotation affects the reader's view of the decision.
guidedPractice.answer: 'Bold' has a positive connotation (brave, confident), while 'reckless' has a negative connotation (dangerous, careless). The author's use of 'bold' frames the decision approvingly, while 'reckless' frames it critically; thus, connotation manipulates reader perception without changing the literal act.

reteachModules.trigger: Student mixes up chronological order with cause-effect or problem-solution, e.g., labeling any ordered list as cause-effect or any problem statement as problem-solution.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Thinks 'sequence' always means cause-effect, or that any text mentioning a problem uses problem-solution, without checking signal words and logical relationships.

miniLesson.explain: Informational texts use different organizational structures for different purposes. Chronological order arranges events by time, using words like 'first,' 'next,' 'then,' and 'finally.' Cause and effect explains why something happened and its result, using words like 'because,' 'so,' and 'therefore.' Problem-solution states a problem and proposes a solution. To identify structure, ask: Is the text mainly showing a time sequence, an explanation of cause/result, or a problem with a fix? Parentheses can add extra context but do not change the main structure.
miniLesson.example: Using the WWI case study: a chronological structure would list 'alliances formed → trench warfare developed → mechanized warfare used → Treaty of Versailles signed.' A cause-effect structure would say 'opposing alliances and mechanized warfare caused a deadly stalemate, leading to the Treaty of Versailles.' The same topic can be presented in different structures depending on the author's purpose.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Ask: Time? Cause? Fix? If you see 'First, then, finally' → chronological. If you see 'because, therefore, as a result' → cause-effect. If you see a problem and a proposed solution → problem-solution.

guidedPractice.prompt: Label each structure: (1) 'Heavy rain flooded the streets, so the city closed the bridges.' (2) 'First, gather supplies; next, build a shelter; finally, wait for rescue.'

A paragraph states: 'Trench warfare created a stalemate on the Western Front. To break it, armies introduced mechanized warfare such as tanks.' Which structure is used, and what clue words or relationships show this?
guidedPractice.answer: Cause and effect. 'Created' shows a cause (trench warfare) and an effect (stalemate); 'to break it' introduces a problem, but the main relationship is cause-effect because it explains why mechanized warfare was introduced.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write one or two sentences using problem-solution structure about the WWI case study, then rewrite the same content using chronological order. Explain how the signal words differ.
guidedPractice.answer: Problem-solution: 'The trench warfare stalemate was a serious problem; the solution was introducing mechanized warfare to break the lines.' Chronological: 'First, opposing alliances formed; then trench warfare created a stalemate; finally, mechanized warfare and the Treaty of Versailles ended the conflict.' Problem-solution uses 'problem/solution' wording; chronological uses time-order words like 'first/then/finally.'

reteachModules.trigger: Student assumes every informational text is neutral and objective, missing value judgments or selective evidence (e.g., answering perspective-driven prose as objective on Q4).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students believe informational texts are simply neutral reports of facts and therefore do not look for the author's perspective, selective evidence, or emotional language.

miniLesson.explain: Objective reporting uses verified facts and a neutral tone. Perspective-driven prose includes personal value judgments and selective evidence. To critically read, identify the author's credentials, target audience, and core communicative purpose rather than assuming neutrality. Even factual-looking text can be one-sided; implicit bias works through omission or one-sided framing and requires cross-source verification.
miniLesson.example: In the WWI case study, a text that says 'the war was a senseless slaughter caused entirely by one nation's aggression' is not objective: it makes a value judgment ('senseless slaughter') and selects only one cause, ignoring that two opposing alliances contributed to the conflict. An objective report would present verified facts about both alliances and the trench warfare stalemate in a neutral tone.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think 'Two mirrors': an objective report reflects facts factually; a perspective-driven text tilts the mirror by choosing which facts to show and adding emotional paint. Always ask 'who wrote this, for whom, and why?'

guidedPractice.prompt:
Which of the following is a clue that a text is perspective-driven rather than objective?
A) It uses verified facts with a neutral tone.
B) It includes personal value judgments and selective evidence.
C) It identifies the author's credentials.
D) It presents multiple viewpoints with citations.

Read this sentence: 'The government's reckless spending on vanity projects has destroyed our economy.' Identify two words that show personal value judgment and state why this is perspective-driven prose.
guidedPractice.answer: 'Reckless' and 'vanity' are emotionally charged value judgments. The sentence also asserts a direct effect without evidence, making it perspective-driven rather than neutral reporting.

guidedPractice.prompt: A newspaper article about the Treaty of Versailles only mentions the damage caused by one country and never mentions the other alliance's actions. Using the critical reading framework, explain how you would determine whether this article is objective or perspective-driven, and what you would do next.
guidedPractice.answer: I would check the author's credentials, target audience, and purpose. Then I'd examine tone and evidence: if the article uses neutral verified facts and includes both sides, it is objective; here it omits the other alliance, which is selective evidence. To verify, I would cross-source with other texts about the WWI case study to see if the omission is consistent or biased.

reteachModules.trigger: When a student attempts to use AI to generate full paragraphs, fake evidence, or other unoriginal work for submission in a critical reading assignment.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may believe AI can be used to generate entire assignments or fabricate evidence without academic integrity consequences.

miniLesson.explain: AI tools can be used as learning partners for structured analysis but must not generate fake evidence or unoriginal student work. Using AI to explain concepts is appropriate, but submitting AI-generated work as your own is plagiarism and academically dishonest.
miniLesson.example: Appropriate: asking AI to explain the difference between explicit and implicit bias so you can write your own analysis. Inappropriate: asking AI to write a full essay or create fake citations.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: AI helps you think, not do your thinking.

guidedPractice.prompt: Is the following action appropriate or inappropriate? A student asks an AI chatbot to explain the difference between explicit and implicit bias so they can write their own summary.
guidedPractice.answer: Appropriate. The student is using AI to understand the concept, but will produce their own work.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain why using AI to generate fake citations is considered academic misconduct, and give one ethical alternative.
guidedPractice.answer: Using AI to generate fake citations fabricates evidence, which is a form of academic dishonesty. An ethical alternative is to use credible sources to find real evidence, and ask the AI only to help you locate or search for sources.

guidedPractice.prompt: A classmate says: 'It's okay if I use AI to write my analysis essay because I'll change some words.' Evaluate this statement using the fact bank guidelines.
guidedPractice.answer: The statement is incorrect. Changing a few words does not make AI-generated work original. Academic integrity requires the work to be your own. AI is a learning partner, not a ghostwriter.

questions.stem: A local news article about a proposed factory includes this sentence: 'The factory will create hundreds of jobs and boost the local economy.' It quotes only the company president and does not mention a residents' protest against pollution. What best describes the bias in this article?
options: No bias, because the sentence uses neutral, factual language.
Explicit bias, because 'hundreds of jobs' is emotionally charged.
Implicit bias, because it omits the residents' perspective and frames the factory only positively.
Bias only if the author uses a negative word like 'dangerous'.

questions.stem: Read this excerpt from an article about a new highway: 'The new highway will shorten commute times by 15 minutes. Local officials say the project is a win for commuters.' A reporter for another paper found that the construction will destroy a park used by many families, but the first article never mentions this. In 2–3 sentences, explain whether this is explicit or implicit bias, what information is omitted, and what strategy a critical reader should use to confirm it.
questions.rubric: Recognizes implicit bias (or not explicit); identifies omitted information (park destruction/families affected); suggests cross-source verification or asking what is missing. Award partial for any two elements.

retestCards.passRule: Must answer Q1 correctly (implicit bias) and demonstrate in Q2 at least two of: classify bias as implicit, identify the omitted perspective, or propose verifying with another source.

questions.stem: Which pair best illustrates the difference between denotation and connotation?
options: "house" (literal: a building for dwelling) vs "home" (emotional: warmth and belonging)
"dog" vs "canine" (both literal, no emotional difference)
"hot" vs "cold" (opposite literal temperatures)
"large" vs "big" (synonyms with the same emotional tone)

questions.stem: A news article calls a protest "a gathering of passionate citizens"; another outlet calls the same event "a mob". What is the main difference?
options: The denotation of "gathering" and "mob" is different; one refers to a larger quantity.
"passionate" and "mob" carry different connotations that shape how readers perceive the event.
"citizens" has no dictionary meaning, so the words are neutral.
There is no meaningful difference; all words in news are objective.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: "The company's new policy was described by supporters as 'flexible' and by critics as 'wishy-washy'." Explain how denotation and connotation work in this sentence. Identify the literal denotation of each word and the emotional connotation each creates.
questions.rubric: Must state that 'flexible' and 'wishy-washy' can share a similar literal meaning (adaptable / lacking firmness), but differ in connotation: 'flexible' has a positive connotation (adaptable, reasonable), while 'wishy-washy' has a negative connotation (indecisive, weak). Must explain that connotation shapes reader perception and that the author's word choice reveals perspective.

retestCards.passRule: All questions must be answered correctly: q1 must select option 0; q2 must select option 1; q3 must explain both the literal meaning and the contrasting connotations of 'flexible' (positive) and 'wishy-washy' (negative) and acknowledge that connotation influences reader perception.

questions.stem: Which signal words or logical relationship best indicate cause-effect structure rather than chronological order?
options: first, next, then, finally
because, therefore, as a result
in addition, for example, also
meanwhile, later, previously

questions.stem: A paragraph states: 'The opposing alliances created dangerous tension. To reduce this risk, diplomats arranged a conference.' Which structure is mainly used?
options: Chronological order
Cause and effect
Problem-solution
Comparison and contrast

questions.stem: Write 1–2 sentences about the WWI case study using problem-solution structure. Then rewrite the same content using chronological order. Briefly explain which signal words or logical relationships you used in each version.
questions.rubric: Problem-solution version states a clear problem and a proposed solution (e.g., 'The trench warfare stalemate was a serious problem; the solution was introducing mechanized warfare to break the lines.'). Chronological version uses time-order markers or sequence (e.g., 'First, alliances formed; then trench warfare caused a stalemate; finally, mechanized warfare and the Treaty of Versailles ended the conflict.'). Explanation correctly identifies problem/solution wording vs time-order words.

retestCards.passRule: q1 and q2 must be correct; q3 must include both a problem-solution sentence and a chronological sentence with appropriate signal words.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the difference between objective reporting and perspective-driven prose?
options: Objective reporting includes the author's opinions; perspective-driven prose uses only facts.
Objective reporting uses verified facts and a neutral tone; perspective-driven prose includes personal value judgments and selective evidence.
Objective reporting always quotes experts; perspective-driven prose never uses evidence.
Objective reporting is only found in textbooks; perspective-driven prose is only in opinion columns.

questions.stem: A blog article about the opening of a new factory states: "The new factory will create hundreds of jobs and boost the local economy. Some residents have raised concerns, but they are simply worried about change." Identify two clues that this article may be perspective-driven rather than objective, and explain what you would do to verify the article's claims.
questions.rubric: The student should identify at least two cues: (1) the dismissive characterization of residents' concerns as 'simply worried about change' is a value judgment, (2) the article omits counterevidence or potential drawbacks, (3) promotional language like 'boost the local economy' presents only positive effects. The verification step should include checking other sources, fact-checking with independent data, or examining the author's credentials/affiliation.

retestCards.passRule: Q1 must have the correct answer (index 1). Q2 must identify at least two perspective-driven cues and propose at least one verification method.

questions.stem: A student is writing a critical reading analysis of a news article. They ask an AI assistant: 'Give me three examples of implicit bias in this article that I can copy into my assignment.' Is this appropriate?
options: Yes, because AI is a tool and using it is allowed.
Yes, if the student changes the wording.
No, because copying AI-generated examples as one's own work is academically dishonest.
No, because AI cannot analyze news articles.

questions.stem: Your friend argues: 'Using AI to generate a full paragraph of analysis is no different from using a calculator in math class.' Write a 2–3 sentence response explaining why this analogy fails, and give one appropriate way to use AI as a learning partner in this course.
questions.rubric: The response must explicitly state that submitting AI-generated work as one's own is academically dishonest, explain that a calculator performs calculations while AI generates reasoning/expression that should be the student's own, and propose an appropriate use such as asking AI to explain concepts, brainstorm ideas, outline, or give feedback—not write the text.

retestCards.passRule: Student must answer Q1 correctly (index 2) and Q2 must state that AI-generated work submitted as own work is academic dishonesty and include at least one appropriate learning-partnership use of AI.

dashboardFormat.objective: To critically read informational texts, identify the author's credentials, target audience, and core communicative purpose rather than assuming neutrality.；Explicit bias uses openly opinionated, inflammatory language; implicit bias relies on fact omission or one-sided framing and requires cross-source verification.；Denotation is a word's literal dictionary meaning, while connotation is its emotional or cultural association; authors choose words to shape reader perception.

cards.question: Which of the following best describes an example of implicit bias in an informational text?
options: Using words like "disastrous" and "horrifying" to describe an event.
Presenting only data that supports one side of an argument while omitting contrary evidence.
Stating "The mayor made a terrible decision" without providing reasons.
Including a headline that says "Shocking Revelation Uncovered!"
cards.diagnosis: Checks if student understands bias is not only explicit but also implicit via omission.
misconceptions: This is explicit bias because the language is openly opinionated and inflammatory.
✓ Correct. Implicit bias often works through omission or one-sided framing rather than obvious emotional words.
This is an explicit opinion, not implicit bias. The author directly states the judgment.
Sensational headlines may grab attention but don't necessarily indicate implicit bias; they are often explicit.
cards.learningGoal: Distinguish between explicit and implicit bias.
cards.successCriteria: Correctly identifies implicit bias as omission or one-sided framing.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
cards.alignmentNote: Directly addresses reading strategies to detect implicit bias.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think bias only appears as explicitly opinionated language.

cards.question: Explain the difference between denotation and connotation, and provide an example of a word whose connotation could change the reader's perception of a news event compared to a neutral synonym.
cards.diagnosis: Checks ability to distinguish between literal and associative word meanings.
cards.learningGoal: Analyze how authors use connotation to shape reader perception.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly defines denotation and connotation and provides a relevant example with explanation.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
cards.alignmentNote: Assesses understanding of language choices in texts.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may conflate denotation and connotation, treating all word meanings as purely literal.

cards.question:
Read the following short passage.

"First, mix the dry ingredients. Next, add the wet ingredients and stir until combined. Then, bake at 350°F for 20 minutes. Finally, let cool before serving."

This passage primarily uses which text structure?
options: Chronological order
Cause and effect
Problem-solution
Compare and contrast
cards.diagnosis: Tests ability to distinguish between text structures like chronological vs cause-effect.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. The passage uses time-order words ("First," "Next," "Then," "Finally") to sequence steps.
Cause and effect would explain why something happens and its result. This passage simply lists steps in order.
Problem-solution would present a problem and propose a solution. There is no problem stated here.
Compare and contrast would highlight similarities and differences between two or more things.
cards.learningGoal: Identify common informational text structures such as chronological order, cause/effect, and problem/solution.
cards.successCriteria: Correctly identifies chronological order from signal words like "first", "next", "then".
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may confuse chronological order with process/sequence or cause-effect when causal language is absent.

cards.question:
Given this short passage:

"The mayor's decision to cut school funding was a heartless move that will devastate the community's future. In reality, proper funding could have been maintained if the council had prioritized education over vanity projects."

Is this objective reporting or perspective-driven prose? Justify your answer with two specific reasons from the text.
cards.diagnosis: Checks if student can differentiate objective from subjective writing by analyzing language.
cards.learningGoal: Distinguish between objective reporting and perspective-driven prose using textual evidence.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies text type and provides two valid reasons from the text.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.
cards.alignmentNote: Assesses ability to recognize textual features of opinion vs fact.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may assume all informational texts are objective and miss value-laden language.

cards.question: Which of the following is an appropriate use of an AI tool for a critical reading assignment?
options: Asking the AI to write a full analysis essay and submitting it as your own work.
Using the AI to generate fake citations to support your argument.
Asking the AI to explain the difference between explicit and implicit bias to help you understand the concept.
Copying an AI-generated summary of a text and presenting it as your own analysis.
cards.diagnosis: Checks understanding that AI should support learning, not replace it.
misconceptions: Submitting AI-generated work as your own is plagiarism and academically dishonest.
Fabricating citations is a serious form of academic misconduct, even if generated by AI.
✓ Correct. Using AI as a learning aid to clarify concepts is ethical, as long as the final submitted work is your own.
Presenting AI-generated content as original work is a violation of academic integrity.
cards.learningGoal: Explain appropriate and ethical uses of AI in critical reading tasks.
cards.successCriteria: Selects the option that uses AI as a learning partner without substituting for original work.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of their own roles and responsibilities in the learning process.
cards.alignmentNote: AI use ties to student responsibility for own learning and academic honesty.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think using AI to generate complete work is acceptable.
